body_html:
The Mind Lies, or La mente miente in Spanish, is my third bilingual book, and it starts from an idea I find both humbling and comforting: your brain is brilliant, ancient and sometimes completely wrong. The book collects 300 short psychology truths about why we think, feel and act the way we do, from overthinking and procrastination to habits, memory, fear, love and happiness. Like my other books, it is written in English with Spanish woven into every page and a Spanish Note on how the language works, so you understand yourself a little better and learn a little Spanish at the same time. Here is why I wrote it.

The book at a glance
  • Title: The Mind Lies | La mente miente
  • What it is: 300 bilingual psychology truths about why we think, feel and act
  • Special pages: “Mind Fact” pages, each explaining one surprising psychology idea
  • Also inside: practical tools, reflection questions and a Spanish Note on every page
  • Length: 304 pages, published in November 2026
{{toc}}

Why I wrote The Mind Lies

Like many people, I have spent too many nights replaying a conversation, worrying about something that never happened, or putting off a task I knew would take ten minutes. At some point I started reading about why our minds do this, and I found the explanations strangely calming. It is not that we are broken. Our brains evolved for a very different world, and many of their shortcuts misfire in modern life.

The more I read, the more I wanted to share those ideas in a simple way. And because I spend my working life between English and Spanish, I wanted to share them in both. The two languages even disagree about the mind in interesting ways: English says you “are” afraid, while Spanish usually says you “have” fear, tengo miedo. Small differences like that make you think about how language shapes the way we describe our inner life.

So The Mind Lies became a book for anyone who has ever argued with their own thoughts, with Spanish as a companion along the way.

What you will find inside

The book covers the everyday patterns most of us struggle with:

  • Overthinking: why the mind loops, and how to step out of it.
  • Habits and procrastination: why good intentions fail, and what small changes help.
  • Memory: why we remember some things vividly and others not at all.
  • Fear and worry: how the brain overestimates danger.
  • Love and relationships: the patterns we bring into them, including attachment styles.
  • Happiness: what actually tends to make people feel better, and what doesn’t.
{{image:2}}

Mind Facts, tools and Spanish Notes

Three kinds of pages run through the book:

  • Mind Fact pages each explain one surprising idea from psychology in plain language. Some famous ones appear, made simple: the spotlight effect (the feeling that everyone notices your mistakes far more than they really do), confirmation bias (our habit of noticing what supports what we already believe) and attachment styles.
  • Practical tools and reflection questions help you apply each idea to your own life, instead of just reading about it.
  • A Spanish Note on every page explains the language behind the idea: how Spanish talks about feelings, which verbs it uses, and the false friends to watch for.

Feelings are a good example of where Spanish differs from English. Spanish often describes emotions with verbs like dar and poner: me da miedo (it scares me), me pone nervioso (it makes me nervous). I wrote a full guide to {{link:talking-about-feelings-in-spanish|talking about feelings in Spanish}} if you want to go further.

A note on what this book is, and isn’t

I am a translator and a writer, not a psychologist, and The Mind Lies is not therapy or medical advice. It is a book of simple, well-known ideas from psychology, explained the way I wish they had been explained to me, to help you notice your own patterns with a little more kindness. If you are struggling with your mental health, please talk to a qualified professional; a book can be a companion, but it is not a replacement for real support.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Why psychology and Spanish go well together

Learning a language means making mistakes in public, and that is exactly where the mind starts lying to us. The spotlight effect convinces you that everyone noticed your wrong verb ending. Fear tells you to stay quiet rather than risk sounding silly. Understanding these patterns makes it easier to keep speaking anyway.

It works the other way too. Reading about your own thoughts in a second language slows you down and makes you pay attention, which is a good habit for both learning and reflection. If mistakes are what stop you from speaking, my guide to {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}} might make you laugh, and remind you that everyone makes them.

Who this book is for

  • Overthinkers, worriers and anyone curious about why they do what they do.
  • Learners with some Spanish who want to read about something interesting, not just practice.
  • Readers who like short, useful nonfiction they can pick up for five minutes.
  • Bilingual households where psychology and feelings are discussed in both languages.
{{image:3}}

How I suggest reading it

Read one page a day, and try the reflection question before moving on. Then look at the Spanish beside the English and read the Spanish Note out loud. If a phrase is useful, like me cuesta trabajo (it’s hard for me) or no le des tantas vueltas (don’t overthink it), save it and use it that week. The combination of a new idea and a new phrase is what makes both stick.

How it fits with my other books

The Mind Lies is the third of my bilingual books. {{link:a-road-in-bloom|A Road in Bloom}} looks at growing up, family, money and peace, and {{link:love-slowly|Love, Slowly}} is about crushes, heartbreak and choosing yourself. They share the same format, so you can read them in any order, and each one stands alone.

A last word

If The Mind Lies helps you catch one unhelpful thought before it runs away with you, and teaches you a few Spanish phrases on the way, it has done its job. I would love to hear which page stayed with you; you can find me on Goodreads.
